lessons.title: The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

before.content_html:
The Five Pillars: The Structure of Muslim Life

The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam are the five core acts of worship and practice that every Muslim is obligated to perform. They are not merely external rituals but the framework through which submission (islam) to Allah is expressed in everyday life. Together they provide a Muslim with a structure that integrates worship, charity, fasting, and pilgrimage into the fabric of existence. The five pillars are: the Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).

The Shahadah

The Shahadah — “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah” — is both the entry point to Islam and its constant foundation. Sincere utterance of the Shahadah constitutes conversion to Islam. The Adhan (call to prayer, which contains the Shahadah) is whispered into the ear of a newborn at birth. The aqiqah — a separate ceremony — is held on the seventh day after birth and includes naming the child. It is recited in the call to prayer five times a day. Many Muslims aspire for the Shahadah to be the final words spoken or heard at death. Reciting the Shahadah in the presence of witnesses marks the formal entry of a convert into the Muslim community (ummah).

Key Fact

The Shahadah (“There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger”) is the first Pillar. It is recited via the Adhan at birth, in every call to prayer, upon conversion, and ideally at death, making it the bookends of Muslim life. The aqiqah is a separate naming ceremony on the seventh day.

Salat: Ritual Prayer Five Times Daily

Salat is the second Pillar and the most visible daily expression of submission to Allah. Muslims are required to pray five times each day: at dawn (Fajr), midday (Zuhr), afternoon (Asr), sunset (Maghrib), and night (Isha). The Qur’an commands prayer and links it directly to moral life: Qur’an 29:45 teaches that prayer restrains one from shameful and unjust deeds. Each prayer involves a set sequence called a rakat (plural: rakat), with physical positions — standing, bowing (ruku’), prostrating (sujud), and sitting — each with specific Arabic phrases. The different prayers require different numbers of rakat (Fajr has two, Zuhr has four, and so on).

Before praying, Muslims must perform wudu (ritual washing), which involves cleaning the hands, mouth, nostrils, face, arms up to the elbow, head, and feet in a prescribed order. Wudu purifies the person physically and mentally, preparing them to stand before Allah. If water is unavailable, a symbolic dry purification using sand or earth (tayammum) is permitted. The worshipper also sets an intention (niyyah) before beginning, ensuring the prayer is a deliberate, conscious act of worship rather than a mechanical routine.

Prayer can be performed anywhere clean (at home, at work, outdoors), with the worshipper facing the direction of Mecca (qibla). Prayer at the mosque, however, is encouraged, especially the Friday midday prayer (Jummah), which is a communal act of worship. The Adhan (call to prayer) is sung from the mosque to signal each prayer time. In addition to Salat, Muslims may also engage in du’ah, which is private, informal supplication — speaking to Allah in one’s own words about personal needs and concerns.

Zakat is the third Pillar — the obligatory payment of a portion of savings to those in need. The standard rate is 2.5% of any savings held for one full lunar year above the minimum threshold (nisab). Zakat may be used for a set list of purposes specified in the Qur’an, including support for the poor, freeing those in debt, and supporting travellers in need. It is not regarded as charity in the Western sense of voluntary generosity; it is a religious duty that purifies wealth. The Arabic word “zakat” means “purification” — giving away a portion of one’s wealth purifies what remains.

In addition to Zakat, Islam strongly encourages voluntary charity called saddaqah. While Zakat is a precise calculation with a fixed rate, saddaqah can be any act of generosity — giving money, sharing food, or even a smile directed at another person. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is reported in the Hadith to have said that every act of goodness is saddaqah.

Sawm is the obligatory fast during the month of Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. Qur’an 2:183 commands the fast: the verse addresses those who believe and commands them to fast as it was prescribed for those before them, so that they may become God-fearing. During Ramadan, adult Muslims abstain from all food, drink (including water), smoking, and sexual relations from the first light of dawn until sunset. The pre-dawn meal (suhoor) sustains them through the day; the fast-breaking meal (iftar) at sunset begins with dates and water, following the Prophet’s example.

The purposes of Sawm are multiple: self-discipline, empathy with those who go hungry, gratitude for Allah’s provision, and heightened spiritual focus. Ramadan is also the month in which the Qur’an was first revealed, making it a time of intensified Qur’an recitation and prayer. Those exempted from fasting include the sick, pregnant or breastfeeding women, travellers, the elderly, and children. Rules about what food is permissible (halal) and forbidden (haram) apply throughout the year; during Ramadan, Muslims pay even closer attention to these boundaries.

Hajj: Pilgrimage to Mecca

Hajj is the fifth Pillar — a pilgrimage to Mecca in Saudi Arabia that every Muslim who is physically able and financially capable must perform at least once in their lifetime. It takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and draws millions of pilgrims from around the world. Qur’an 3:97 underlines the duty of pilgrimage for those who are able. The Hajj commemorates the trials of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his family, and the events it re-enacts are rooted in the pre-Islamic history of Mecca.

On arrival in Mecca, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity (ihram), wearing two plain white sheets that remove all distinctions of wealth, nationality, and status. Key rituals of the Hajj include: circling the Ka’bah seven times (tawaf); walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa; standing in prayer at the plain of Arafah; throwing stones at three pillars in Mina to symbolise rejecting the devil (Shaytan); and the sacrifice of an animal (qurbani) commemorating Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son. The pilgrimage concludes with the celebration of Id-ul-Adha. Hajj powerfully demonstrates the equality of all Muslims before Allah and the unity of the global Muslim community (ummah).

Key Fact

The Five Pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salat (five daily prayers), Zakat (2.5% alms tax), Sawm (Ramadan fast, commanded in Qur’an 2:183), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). Together they form the practical structure of Muslim life and submission to Allah.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Five Pillars — Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj — form the core obligations of Sunni Muslim life. Each integrates worship with ethics: Salat restrains sin (Qur’an 29:45), Zakat purifies wealth, Sawm builds God-consciousness (Qur’an 2:183), and Hajj unites the ummah.
  • Salat requires wudu (ritual washing) and niyyah (intention) before five daily prayers, each consisting of set rakat. The Friday Jummah prayer at the mosque is a communal obligation for men. Du’ah is additional personal supplication.
  • Hajj to Mecca is obligatory for those able to undertake it. Pilgrims wear identical ihram garments, removing all distinctions of status, and re-enact the trials of Ibrahim, affirming the unity and equality of the global Muslim community.

before.content_html:
Prophethood — Risalah

Risalah is the Arabic term for prophethood. Muslims believe God has sent a series of prophets to guide human beings at different times in history. The Qur’an teaches that Muslims should make no distinction between the prophets: the passage at surah 2, verse 136 states that believers say they have faith in God and in what was revealed to Ibrahim (Abraham), Ishmael, Ishaq (Isaac), Yaqub (Jacob), and the tribes, and in what was given to Musa (Moses), Isa (Jesus) and all the other prophets. This verse is one of the key scriptural anchors for the doctrine of Risalah.

Key Fact

Islam recognises a long chain of prophets from Adam to Muhammad. Muhammad is called Khatam an-Nabiyyin — the Seal of the Prophets — meaning no prophet will come after him. This is a central belief that distinguishes Islam from traditions that recognise later prophetic figures.

The Key Prophets

Adam is regarded as the first human being and the first prophet. Muslims believe God created Adam from clay and breathed life into him, appointing him as God’s representative (khalifah) on earth. Adam’s story establishes the human being’s accountability to God from the very beginning.

Ibrahim (Abraham) holds a uniquely important place in Islam. He is regarded as the father of monotheism — the belief in one God. Ibrahim rejected idol worship and, together with his son Ishmael, is believed to have rebuilt the Ka’bah in Mecca as a house of worship dedicated to God alone. His willingness to sacrifice his son at God’s command is commemorated every year at the festival of Id-ul-Adha.

Isa (Jesus) is honoured as a prophet and the Messiah in Islam, though Muslims do not believe he is divine or the Son of God. Surah 2, verse 87 of the Qur’an confirms that God gave Isa clear signs and supported him with the Holy Spirit. Muslims believe Isa was born of a virgin (Maryam), performed miracles by God’s permission, and was raised to God rather than crucified — a view that contrasts sharply with Christian doctrine.

Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the final prophet. Born in Mecca around 570 CE, he received the Qur’an through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) over approximately 23 years. Muslims regard the Qur’an as the direct, unchanged word of God — the final revelation. As Khatam an-Nabiyyin, Muhammad’s message is believed to be the complete and perfect version of the guidance that earlier prophets brought in part.

Al-Qadr means divine predestination or decree. Muslims believe God has knowledge of all things, past, present and future, and that nothing happens outside God’s will. This is one of the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam.

The relationship between al-Qadr and human free will is a profound theological question. Most Muslim scholars hold that God’s foreknowledge of events does not remove human responsibility — people still make genuine choices and will be held accountable for them. On the Day of Judgement, every person will be asked about the choices they freely made, even though God knew what those choices would be. Al-Qadr therefore calls Muslims to trust in God while taking full moral responsibility for their actions.

Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means ‘the hereafter’ or life after death. It is one of the most important Islamic beliefs and shapes how Muslims live in this world. The Qur’an teaches extensively about what follows death, including the nature of Yawm al-Qiyamah (the Day of Judgement), and the existence of Jannah (paradise) and Jahannam (hell). Surah 46, verse 33 and surah 3, verse 16 are among the passages the spec highlights as scriptural anchors for this doctrine.

Key Fact

Yawm al-Qiyamah is the Day of Judgement. Muslims believe every person who has ever lived will be resurrected. Their deeds will be weighed and they will answer for every choice they made. Those whose good deeds outweigh their sins will enter Jannah; those whose sins are heavier will face Jahannam.

Jannah is described in the Qur’an in rich, vivid terms — a place of peace, flowing water, companionship and nearness to God. The highest reward is not merely comfort but the direct experience of God’s presence. Jahannam is a place of punishment, described using imagery of fire and torment. Many Muslim scholars interpret these descriptions both literally and symbolically — as real consequences of rejecting God’s guidance. The belief in akhirah motivates Muslims to act justly and generously in this life, because they know they will be held accountable.

The mosque (masjid) is the centre of Muslim community life. Its key architectural features carry significant symbolic meaning. The mihrab is a niche in the wall pointing towards Mecca, indicating the direction (qibla) Muslims must face when praying. The minbar is the raised pulpit from which the imam delivers the Friday sermon (khutbah). Many mosques also have a dome — a practical feature that amplifies sound — and a minaret from which the call to prayer (adhan) is traditionally broadcast.

Mosques serve a range of community functions beyond daily prayer: they host Qur’an classes, Eid gatherings, marriages, funerals, and welfare support. In this way, the mosque embodies the concept of ummah — the global community of Muslims united in faith.

Clothing and Identity

Muslim women’s dress is a topic of real diversity within Islam. The hijab covers the hair and neck. The niqab covers the face except for the eyes. The burkha is a full body covering including a mesh over the eyes. Different Muslim communities interpret modesty requirements differently. Some women wear the hijab as a personal act of faith and identity; others see all forms of face covering as a matter of personal choice; some Muslim scholars argue that only modest dress (not necessarily a specific garment) is required. The diversity of practice within Muslim communities reflects the range of interpretations of Qur’anic guidance on modesty.

Lesser Jihad

The word jihad means ‘struggle’ or ‘striving’. Muslims distinguish between the greater jihad (the inner spiritual struggle to live a righteous life) and the lesser jihad (the external struggle, which can in certain circumstances include armed defence). The Qur’an sets strict conditions for the lesser jihad: surah 2, verse 190 states that Muslims should fight in God’s cause against those who fight them, but should not begin hostilities. The conditions for declaring a lesser jihad are demanding — it must be defensive, declared by legitimate authority, use proportionate force, and avoid harming non-combatants. This contrasts with popular misconceptions that equate jihad simply with warfare.

Islamic Festivals

Id-ul-Adha (the Festival of Sacrifice) commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son at God’s command. Muslims across the world slaughter an animal (if they are able), divide the meat into three parts — for the family, neighbours and the poor — and attend special prayers. It coincides with the end of the Hajj pilgrimage.

Id-ul-Fitr (the Festival of Breaking the Fast) marks the end of Ramadan. Muslims gather for communal prayers, exchange gifts and meals, pay Zakat al-Fitr (a special charitable contribution) and celebrate the completion of a month of fasting and increased devotion. Both festivals reinforce the sense of ummah — community solidarity that transcends national and cultural boundaries.

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) falls within the last ten nights of Ramadan. Muslims believe this is the night on which the first verses of the Qur’an were revealed to Muhammad. Many Muslims spend the night in prayer, Qur’an recitation and reflection. The Qur’an describes this night as ‘better than a thousand months’ (surah 97), making it the most spiritually significant night of the Islamic calendar.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of a mosque.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of the following: mihrab (niche pointing to Mecca / qibla direction); minbar (raised pulpit for Friday sermon); minaret (tower for the call to prayer); dome; wudu (ablution) area; separate prayer areas for men and women.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'Risalah' mean in Islam?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: prophethood / the belief that God has sent messengers (prophets) to guide humanity. One mark for a partial answer such as 'messengers of God' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Muslim beliefs about the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Qiyamah).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description covering resurrection of all souls, weighing of deeds, accountability for choices made in life, entry to Jannah for the righteous and Jahannam for the wicked, with explanation of why this belief matters (motivates just living, connects to al-Qadr). Secure: Clear description of resurrection, judgement and outcomes (Jannah/Jahannam) with some explanation. Developing: Basic description of judgement with limited detail. Emerging: Simple statement that Muslims believe in a Day of Judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the festivals of Id-ul-Adha and Id-ul-Fitr influence Muslim practice today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains what each festival commemorates (Ibrahim's sacrifice; end of Ramadan), describes key practices (animal sacrifice, Zakat al-Fitr, communal prayer, gift-giving), and explains the influence on Muslim life today (reinforcing ummah, expressing gratitude, fulfilling religious duty, demonstrating social responsibility to the poor). Secure: Clear explanation of both festivals with developed points about influence. Developing: Basic description of one or both festivals; limited explanation of influence. Emerging: Names one festival with little development.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Muslim beliefs about the afterlife (akhirah).
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs, each linked to a source of authority. E.g. Belief 1: Jannah (paradise) is a place of peace and nearness to God — the Qur'an (3:16) describes God's reward for those who are mindful of Him. Belief 2: Jahannam (hell) is the consequence of rejecting God's guidance — surah 46:33 reminds believers that God who created them has the power to raise the dead. Concludes by connecting akhirah to al-Qadr and human accountability. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one source; some development of each. Developing: Two beliefs stated but one or both lack development or source. Emerging: One belief mentioned with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'Muslims who believe in al-Qadr cannot truly be held responsible for their actions.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument engaging with the tension between divine foreknowledge and human free will. Arguments in support: al-Qadr states God decrees all things; if God knows what will happen, human choice seems determined; some fatalist readings suggest events are 'written'. Arguments against: mainstream Muslim scholarship holds God's foreknowledge does not remove human free will; Muslims are taught to make genuine choices and will be judged on them (Yawm al-Qiyamah); the Qur'an commands right action repeatedly, implying humans can choose. Non-religious view: secular humanists affirm full human moral responsibility without reference to divine decree. Justified conclusion with personal stance. Secure: Two developed arguments (agree/disagree) with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides but little evaluation or no source. Emerging: One-sided or descriptive answer.
